newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour Party assures business the left is dead.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour Party assures business the left is dead.

text.p: Business has come to terms with the idea that centrist Labour leader Tony Blair will be Britain's next prime minister, but some industrialists still worry the party's left wing is simply lying low until after the election.
At a conference last week on the implications of a Labour government for business, Stephen Byers, who speaks for the party on trade union matters, said such fears were misplaced.

There would be 80 or 90 new members of parliament on the Labour benches after the election, due by May 22, he said. "Almost without exception, they share the values I have outlined this morning, and are supporters of Tony Blair," Byers added.
Phil Cole, once a Labour insider and now a lobbyist with public relations firm Burson-Marsteller, confirmed that picture.

"This generation will not be disposed to wear badges of left orthodoxy. The dominant political stance is overwhelmingly pro-leadership. The new intake will see only three or four candidates really comfortable wearing a left label," he said.
Specific issues rankle with industry, not least a plan to slap a levy on the excess profits of privatised utilities.

Kate Barker, chief economist with the main employers' group, the Confederation of British Industry, said the retrospective windfall tax set "a very disturbing precedent for people who are thinking of investing in the UK".
But analysts told the conference the utilities could afford the three billion pounds ($4.9 billion) or more likely to be levied, and the companies themselves seemed resigned to paying.
"We think it should be fairly applied and reasonably calculated. It's not a question of fighting it," said John Devaney of Eastern Group, an electricity supplier.
The other main gripe was the minimum wage Labour has pledged to introduce after taking soundings from industry and unions.

But Christopher Haskins, chief executive of Northern Foods, a major British food producer, said there would be no impact on industry or employment if the minimum was no higher than 4.25 pounds an hour, around the level sought by the unions.
"I think most employers would be pleased they would not have cut-throat competition to deal with," he said.
Labour has also pledged to sign up to the Social Chapter, which sets minimum standards for workers in the European Union.

The Conservative government has negotiated an opt-out from the Chapter and Prime Minister John Major claims that signing up for it would destroy half a million jobs. Employment specialists ridiculed that figure, noting the Chapter had only spawned works councils -- consultative bodies meeting once a year -- and a right to unpaid parental leave.

"There is a worry... that it (the Social Chapter) will be used as a Trojan horse to introduce a whole raft of new measures, but there's no political impetus in Europe to do that," Labour's Byers said.

The conference was organised by a free-market think tank, the Adam Smith Institute, but Labour spokesmen seemed entirely at ease -- a reflection of how far the party has travelled from its socialist roots since Blair became leader in 1994.

Labour trade spokesman Stuart Bell threw in a mischievous reference to (the late Chinese leader) Mao Zedong, but ultimately he too had a soothing message. "Under New Labour none of you will be wearing Chinese tunics," he reassured the pin-striped businessmen. ($1=.6167 Pound)
